title: EventEmitter
lede: Node's classic EventEmitter, not the WHATWG EventTarget/Event trio. The big divergence is that it's a compiler-recognized generic built-in (monomorphized per T like Map/Set/Promise), not a real registered class — so the on/once/emit/off surface is hand-written codegen dispatched by name and instanceof answers as a compile-time constant. A subclass can still override any of those methods (the override wins at every call site, and super.<method>(...) reaches the built-in). Payloads are statically typed through an event-map type argument, with tuple payloads standing in for Node's multi-argument events.

entries.name: new EventEmitter<T>() / class X extends EventEmitter<T>
entries.statusRow: new EventEmitter<T>() / extending it via class X extends EventEmitter<T>
entries.signature: new EventEmitter<T>(); class X extends EventEmitter<T> {}
entries.description: Either construct a standalone emitter or root a class in one via extends — the subclass then gets the whole on/once/emit/off/removeListener/removeAllListeners/listenerCount/eventNames surface for free. T is the event-payload type: a scalar/Error for a single shared payload, or an object type mapping each event name to its own payload.

returns.desc: An emitter, or a subclass instance rooted in one.

differences: A subclass may override any EventEmitter method (`on`/`once`/`emit`/`off`/`removeListener`/`removeAllListeners`/`listenerCount`/`eventNames`) — the override wins at every call site (statically and virtually), and `super.<method>(...)` reaches the nearest ancestor override or the built-in dispatch. The override's declared signature isn't checked against the built-in it replaces

entries.name: .on(event, listener) / .once(event, listener)
entries.signature: .on(event: string, listener: (...args) => void): this; .once(event, listener): this
entries.description: Registers a listener for an event; once fires at most once then detaches itself. Both are chainable, returning the emitter. The listener's parameters come from the event's declared payload type — one parameter per tuple element, a single parameter for a scalar payload, or none for a void event.

params.name: event
params.desc: Event name (a string literal for a map-typed emitter).

params.name: listener
params.desc: Callback whose params match the event's payload type.

differences: A **tuple** payload `[A, B, …]` is Node's multi-argument event — the listener takes one parameter per element (`(a, b) => …`); a non-tuple payload is a single argument (or none, for `void`). No open-ended `(...args)` beyond a declared tuple
A map-typed emitter requires a string-literal event name at every call site

entries.name: .emit(event, ...args)
entries.description: Synchronously invokes every listener registered for event, in registration order, passing along the arguments. Returns whether any listener ran. A tuple-payload event takes one argument per element; a scalar payload takes a single data argument.

params.name: event
params.desc: Event name (a string literal for a map-typed emitter).

params.name: args
params.desc: Payload — one arg per tuple element, or a single value.

returns.desc: true if at least one listener ran.

differences: Multi-argument `emit(event, a, b, …)` for an event whose payload is a tuple `[A, B, …]`; a non-tuple payload takes one data argument. Open-ended untyped varargs (beyond a declared tuple) aren't supported
A map-typed emitter requires a string-literal event name

entries.name: .off / .removeListener / .removeAllListeners
entries.description: Detaches listeners. off and removeListener remove a single listener from an event. removeAllListeners with no argument clears every event; passed an event name, it clears just that one.

params.name: event
params.desc: Event name; omitted on removeAllListeners to clear all.

params.name: listener
params.desc: The exact listener reference to remove.

entries.name: .listenerCount(event) / .eventNames()
entries.description: listenerCount reports how many listeners are registered for an event. eventNames returns the names that currently have listeners, in registration order — an implementation detail of the underlying map, not a documented ordering guarantee.

returns.desc: The listener count, or the array of event names.

entries.name: emit('error', ...) special-case
entries.signature: .emit('error', payload): boolean  // throws if no 'error' listener
entries.description: Matches Node's one specially treated event name: emitting 'error' with no registered 'error' listener throws instead of silently swallowing the problem, so a forgotten handler fails loudly. Resolved entirely at the emit call site — no runtime cost when the event name isn't 'error' beyond the strcmp itself.

returns.desc: As emit — but throws when 'error' has no listener.

entries.name: events.once()
entries.description: Returns a Promise that resolves with the event's argument array the first time it fires.
entries.snippet:
import { EventEmitter, once } from 'events'
const ee = new EventEmitter<{ ready: [number] }>()
setTimeout(() => { ee.emit('ready', 42) }, 0)
const arr = await once(ee, 'ready') // [42]
differences: Single-value / homogeneous multi-arg events only (mixed-type tuples rejected)

entries.name: events.on()
entries.description: Returns an async iterator that yields the event's argument array on each emission, buffering events that arrive between iterations and parking the consumer when the queue drains. The listener attaches eagerly at the on(...) call, so events emitted before consumption starts are buffered rather than lost.

returns.desc: An async iterator yielding each emission's argument array.

differences: Same payload rules as once: single-value / homogeneous multi-arg events only
The buffer is unbounded (Node's default); iterator .return()/.throw() unregistering the listener is a deferred follow-up
